newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, Britain still at odds over BA-American link-up.
newsitem.headline: EU, Britain still at odds over BA-American link-up.

text.p: Britain and the European Commission are still at loggerheads over the proposed alliance between British Airways Plc and AMR's American Airlines but at least they are talking.

"Contact has resumed (between the Commission and the UK authorities) but positions still differ widely on the substance of the case," European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a meeting of the European Parliament's Transport Committee.
Van Miert again warned the British government against reaching a decision on the alliance which would not fully meet the Commission's competition concerns.
If this were to happen, the Commission itself would take "a negative decision" and recommend that the other EU countries take the necessary steps to avoid the deal coming into force in their markets.
"One should be fully aware of this possibility", he said.

The Commission has taken the view that the alliance would harm competition, particularly on the routes between Britain and the United States where the two airlines would control 61 percent of passenger transport.
They would also have a monopoly position of 13 UK-U.S. routes including London and New York's JFK airport.

Van Miert said Britain's preliminary decision to give conditional clearance to the alliance, which was announced by the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) in December, "was far from meeting (the Commission's) concerns".
The OFT said BA and American must give up 168 weekly slots at the congested London Heathrow airport.
Van Miert said he thought "it would probably have to be more than that", but declined to put a figure on it.

"There are elements which need to be discussed, such as the number of slots," he told the committee, after several questions on the conditions the Commission was likely to impose in return for its approval.
But he made it crystal clear that the Commission would not allow the slots to be sold. EU legislation currently being revised only provides for the exchange of slots.

Both Van Miert and transport commissioner Neil Kinnock, who shares responsibility for vetting the BA-American deal and a string of other transatlatic alliances, said the final decision could come within a month.
Before that, the Commission will ask national experts from the 15 EU states to give their opinion, which could happen within weeks, Van Miert said.
Van Miert said the Commission still needed more information on the alliance, despite having already received written and oral answers from both companies to its objections.

The Commission's authority to investigate the deal has been openly challenged by BA and the British government. Both argue the British antitrust authorities have a greater say than the Commission, whose jurisdiction only applies clearly to deals involving EU-based carriers.
But the Commission points out that the deal would affect traffic with mainland Europe, not just Britain.
"The effects of this agreement will be felt in the whole Union, not just Britain," Van Miert said.

In a move to avoid future jurisdictional conflicts with national governments, Van Miert announced the Commission would "soon" propose modifying EU air transport legislation to cover services with non-EU countries.
Any changes will have to be approved by EU transport ministers.
The Commission started separate probes in July into several transatlantic air deals but the BA-American link-up is the only one to have attracted headlines because it is the largest.

Tension mounted in January between the Commission and the British government when the Commission bluntly threatened to go to the European Court of Justice if its competition concerns were not given apropriate attention.
Antitrust authorities on both sides now seem to be co-operating a lot more, although Van Miert's comments made it clear that differences had not been ironed out.

The alliance also faces a regulatory hurdle in the United States where it has been made conditional to the conclusion of an "open skies" agreement opening up the UK-U.S. aviation market to competing airlines.
